item.title: Kirishima Hot Spring Resort — Guide
item.description: The Kirishima hot-spring area, spread across the volcanic slopes at the foot of the Kirishima mountains, is one of southern Kyushu’s finest onsen destinations. Fed by the region’s intense volcanic activity, the springs here are abundant and varied, including prized cloudy, milky-white sulphur waters that are rich in minerals and wonderfully soothing. Ryokan, hotels and public baths are dotted through the forested highlands and gorges, many with open-air baths (rotenburo) where you can soak in the hot mineral waters surrounded by mountain scenery, greenery and, in places, the sounds of a river or waterfall.

item.title: Kirishima Mountains & Onsen — Guide
item.description: The Kirishima area, straddling the border of Kagoshima and Miyazaki, is a dramatic volcanic landscape of peaks, craters and crater lakes protected within Japan’s first national park, and a wonderful mountain and onsen destination. Its cluster of volcanoes includes the highest peak Karakuni-dake and the conical Takachiho-no-mine, considered sacred as the mythological spot where the grandson of the sun goddess is said to have descended to earth — a legend enshrined at the ancient, vermilion Kirishima Jingū shrine on the wooded slopes.

item.title: Kirishima Mountains — Guide
item.description: The Kirishima Mountains, a cluster of volcanic peaks straddling the border between Miyazaki and Kagoshima, form one of Kyushu’s most dramatic and spiritually significant landscapes, protected within Japan’s first national park. This still-active volcanic range features more than twenty craters, several vivid blue-green crater lakes, steaming vents and rugged peaks including Karakuni-dake (the highest) and the perfectly conical Mount Takachiho-no-mine. The mountains are laced with hiking trails offering superb views over craters, lakes and, on clear days, all the way to the sea and the volcano of Sakurajima.

item.title: Minami Aso Museum & Volcano Science — Guide
item.description: In Minami-Aso (‘southern Aso’), on the floor of the great caldera, this museum introduces the geology, volcanoes, nature and water of the Aso region through accessible exhibits. Aso’s landscape is the product of colossal ancient eruptions and ongoing volcanic activity, and the museum helps visitors understand how the vast caldera formed, how the still-active Nakadake volcano behaves, and how the region’s ecosystems and famous pure spring water are shaped by this volcanic land.

item.title: Mount Aso and Nakadake Crater — Guide
item.description: Mount Aso (Aso-san), in the centre of Kumamoto, is one of the world’s most active volcanoes and the beating heart of the region. It sits within one of the largest volcanic calderas on Earth — a vast basin, formed by ancient super-eruptions, that today holds towns, farms and railways ringed by the caldera’s grassy rim. At its centre rise five volcanic peaks, of which Nakadake is still highly active. When conditions allow, visitors can go right up to the rim of Nakadake’s crater and peer down at a steaming, otherworldly turquoise pool of volcanic water, ringed by barren ash-grey slopes and rising fumes — a raw, unforgettable sight found in few other places.

item.title: Sakurajima Volcano — Guide
item.description: Sakurajima is one of the world’s most active volcanoes and the iconic symbol of Kagoshima, looming dramatically across Kinko Bay from the city. This towering volcanic peak erupts frequently — sometimes puffing plumes of ash over the city daily — and a lava flow in 1914 was so vast it joined the former island to the Osumi Peninsula. Despite its fury, people live on its slopes, and it’s easily and safely visited by a short, scenic ferry from Kagoshima city (running 24 hours).

item.title: Mt. Chokai (Dewa Fuji): Akita's Coastal Volcano — Guide
item.description: Mt. Chokai is a majestic 2,236 m volcano rising straight from the coast on the Akita–Yamagata border — the ‘Dewa Fuji’. Its upper slopes hold alpine meadows and snow patches into summer, and clear-day panoramas sweep across the Sea of Japan. Multiple trails climb from both prefectures; the Akita-side Hokodate route is popular in the July–September season. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Nikaho, Akita Hours Hiking season ~Jul–Sep Admission Free Time needed Full day (summit) Best time Summer (alpine flowers) What to See The 2,236 m ‘Dewa Fuji’ rising from the coast.

item.title: Mt. Iwaki (Tsugaru Fuji): Aomori's Sacred Cone — Guide
item.description: Mt. Iwaki, affectionately called ‘Tsugaru Fuji’, is the graceful 1,625 m volcano that towers over Hirosaki’s apple orchards. A skyline toll road and near-summit chairlift make its panoramas easy to reach, while hikers can climb from Iwakiyama Shrine at its base. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hirosaki, Aomori Hours Skyline road ~Apr–Oct, daytime Admission Toll road/chairlift fees apply Time needed Half day Best time Summer & autumn (road open) What to See Sweeping summit-area panoramas over the Tsugaru plain.

item.title: Mt. Iwate (Nambu Fuji): Tohoku's Iconic Volcano — Guide
item.description: Mt. Iwate, known as ‘Nambu Fuji’ for its near-perfect cone, is Iwate’s iconic 2,038 m stratovolcano and a symbol of the prefecture. The summer hiking season (July–October) offers crater-rim walks with sweeping views across the Kitakami basin; the popular Umagaeshi trail reaches the summit in about 4–5 hours. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Shizukuishi, Iwate Hours Hiking season ~Jul–Oct Admission Free Time needed Full day (summit hike) Best time Summer–autumn (hiking) What to See The near-perfect ‘Nambu Fuji’ cone, Iwate’s symbol.
